replying_to: Replying to Personalized Federated Learning with Clustered Generalization
display_title: Official Review of Paper2546 by Reviewer 13vq

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper wants to introduce a new personalization approach for federated learning based on the clustering of clients. The clustering is being done on the model parameters space to categorize similar models together. They formulate this problem as a bilevel optimization and add a regularization term similar to pFedMe algorithm for the sake of personalization.  Using the clustering, they show that convergence rate can have $\sqrt{K}$ speedup over non-clustered federated learning. Through several experimental results, mostly compared with pFedMe algorithm they show improvement on different datasets.
content.main_review:
The main concern for the proposal of CGPFL, similar to the pFedMe is that adding the regularization term of $\ell_2$ distance to the global model or the cluster center does not seem to be the goal of personalization. This regularization term, similar to FedProx [A] or to some extent SCAFFOLD [B] intends to keep the local model close to the global model and acts as a variance reduction step. This seems to be effective for general federated learning algorithms, however, it has the opposite goal of personalization, since it does not consider the local optimal of each client. However, this is less of an issue here since the cluster center are better utilized for each cluster data distribution. Hence, I expect to see more comparison with other PFL methods than pFedMe to have a better comparison. 

In addition, they provide a generalization bound, however, they do not mention two other prior work in this domain [C] and [D], which provide extensive generalization analysis of their personalization approaches. There is no comparison with them in this regard and how they are improving their generalization bound.

Moreover, in the convergence analysis, they are claiming that they can achieve $\sqrt{K}$ speedup over other methods. This is the vanishing term in the convergence rate. However, from the experimental results in Figure 1, it seems that there is a gap between the non vanishing bias term in the convergence of CGPFL and pFedMe.  Is this validated by the theory as well? From the convergence analysis of pFedMe, this seems to be the case, but is this the case for other PFL methods? That is another reason, I think the experimental results should contain other PFL methods as well.

Also, there are some discrepancy on the results of for some methods mentioned in this paper and their reported numbers. For instance for APFL[C], for the logistic regression on MNIST with 2 classes per client (they have 100 client, which is harder than 40 clients in CGPFL), and they are getting about 97.5% accuracy on personalized models on validation data, while you report 92.69%. Also, for the CIFAR10 on CNN models, they report 89.33%, which is way different from what is reported here. This discrepancy should be addressed.


[A] Li, Tian, et al. "Federated optimization in heterogeneous networks." arXiv preprint arXiv:1812.06127 (2018).

[B] Karimireddy, Sai Praneeth, et al. "SCAFFOLD: Stochastic Controlled Averaging for On-Device Federated Learning." (2019).

[C] Deng, Yuyang, Mohammad Mahdi Kamani, and Mehrdad Mahdavi. "Adaptive personalized federated learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2003.13461 (2020).

[D] Mansour, Yishay, et al. "Three approaches for personalization with applications to federated learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.10619 (2020).

1. Q: Hence, I expect to see more comparison with other PFL methods than pFedMe to have a better comparison.

A: We have made more comparisons with other PFL methods and the results are updated into the Figure 1 and Figure 2 in the revision paper. You can check them in the latest version.

2. Q: In addition, they provide a generalization bound, however, they do not mention two other prior work in this domain [C] and [D], which provide extensive generalization analysis of their personalization approaches. There is no comparison with them in this regard and how they are improving their generalization bound.

A: We don't guarantee the improvement of generalization bound over the mentioned two works [C][D], while we guarantee the improvement of generalization bound over the global-model-regularized PFL methods, e.g., [E][F][G]. In this work, the generalization bound is derived to seek the optimal generalization-personalization trade-off in global-model-regularized PFLs. To improve the generalization bound against other related works deserves more efforts in our future works.

3. Q: Moreover, in the convergence analysis, they are claiming that they can achieve  speedup over other methods. This is the vanishing term in the convergence rate. However, from the experimental results in Figure 1, it seems that there is a gap between the non vanishing bias term in the convergence of CGPFL and pFedMe. Is this validated by the theory as well? From the convergence analysis of pFedMe, this seems to be the case, but is this the case for other PFL methods? That is another reason, I think the experimental results should contain other PFL methods as well.

A: a. For the non vanishing bias term, I think that you refer to the bias between the stable accuracy/loss when the models finally converge. It is validated by the theory in Section 4.3. Because our method can reach a better trade-off (near-optimal) between personalization and generalization for the personalized models, it can achieve a higher stable accuracy than other PFLs that are regularized by a single global model. The generalization bound in Section 4.3 is introduced to demonstrate that our method can reach a better trade-off (near-optimal) between personalization and generalization. Moreover, the non vanishing bias term exactly support our claim 'better personalization-generalization trade-off can lead to higher model accuracy'.

b. We have made more comparisons with other PFL methods and the results are updated into the Figure 1 and Figure 2 in the revision paper. You can check them.

4. Q: Also, there are some discrepancy on the results of for some methods mentioned in this paper and their reported numbers. For instance for APFL[C], for the logistic regression on MNIST with 2 classes per client (they have 100 client, which is harder than 40 clients in CGPFL), and they are getting about 97.5\% accuracy on personalized models on validation data, while you report 92.69\%. Also, for the CIFAR10 on CNN models, they report 89.33\%, which is way different from what is reported here.

A: To guarantee the fairness between different methods, we set the same hyperparameters (e.g., $N$, $T$, $R$ and $lr$) in those methods with same values which cannot guarantee the optimal performance reported in APFL[C]. content.title: Response to the rebuttal
content.comment:
Thanks for your supportive comments and valuable suggestions. Thanks for your re-rating of this paper. Here are our responses to your remaining concerns.

**Q: The discussion and explanation regarding the generalization bound should be added to the paper with more details, because I believe this is the most important part for a personalization method than the convergence rate analysis.**

**A:**

1. **For convergence rate.** The speedup of convergence rate is much more important in FL setting than in centralized setting. There is no doubt that the generalization bound is one of the most important topics in PFL. Meanwhile, the convergence rate is also of great importance in federated learning (FL). Compared with the traditional centralized training mode, one of the most significant bottlenecks in FL is the communication [7]. The convergence rate determines how many communication rounds are needed to achieve a high model accuracy in FL. Therefore, the theoretical analysis on convergence rate is neccessary for FL, and the speedup of convergence rate is much more important in FL setting than in centralized setting. Our proposed CGPFL provides theoretical guarantee of convergence rate, which achieves $\sqrt{K}$ times speedup over the state-of-the-art PFL methods.

2. **For generalization bound.** In this work, the generalization bound is **mainly introduced as a tool** to demonstrate the existence of the optimal personalization-generalization trade-off and to inspire the algorithm to reach a near-optimal trade-off. We only improve the generalization bound, compared with other $L2$-norm regularized PFL methods ([1][2][3][4]). It's limited because there are still some other directions in PFL, such as model interpolation [5] and clustering + local fine-tuning [6]. Improving the generalization bound in a more general FL framework can be the future direction.

**Q: From the Table 1. it seems that in most experiments APFL is the best SOTA method among different methods and datasets. However, the authors have chosen other algorithms to compare with in the rest of the paper. Also, each of these methods has some hyperparameters that I think should be mentioned in the paper, to see if they are tuned based on the optimal performance or not.**

**A:**

1. From the Table 1, APFL does achieve the best SOTA accuracy on several datasets. However, as reported in other papers [1], APFL didn't outperform Ditto [1] on model accuracy. Based on our investigation, we believe that the reason may come from the similar data partitioning law in this paper and APFL. Therefore, we only choose Ditto, pFedMe and Per-FedAvg as the representative PFL methods in the rest of the paper.

2. As discussed in [5], the convergence rate of APFL depends on the value of $\alpha$. It's difficult to compare the covergence rate of APFL and our method on a fair criterion. If we use the optimal $\alpha$, it is unfair for our method with fixed $K=2,4,8$. If we randomly choose a value for $\alpha$, it is unfair for APFL. The rest of this paper aims at showing the convergence rate and the effect of $K$ for CGPFL, therefore we don't include the method APFL.

3. We have included most of the hyperparameters and discussed the most important ones in the main text. Of course, we will provide all of the chosen values of hyperparameters in appendix of the final version if there are still some omissions in the current version.

[1] Li, T., Hu, S., Beirami, A., \& Smith, V. (2021, July). Ditto: Fair and robust federated learning through personalization. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 6357-6368). PMLR.

[2] T Dinh, C., Tran, N., \& Nguyen, T. D. (2020). Personalized Federated Learning with Moreau Envelopes. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 33.

[3] Hanzely, F., \& Richtárik, P. (2020). Federated learning of a mixture of global and local models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.05516.

[4] Hanzely, F., Hanzely, S., Horváth, S., \& Richtarik, P. (2020). Lower Bounds and Optimal Algorithms for Personalized Federated Learning. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 33.

[5] Yuyang Deng, Mohammad Mahdi Kamani, and Mehrdad Mahdavi. Adaptive personalized federated learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2003.13461, 2020.

[6] Yishay Mansour, Mehryar Mohri, Jae Ro, and Ananda Theertha Suresh. Three approaches for personalization with applications to federated learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.10619, 2020.

[7] McMahan, B., Moore, E., Ramage, D., Hampson, S., \& y Arcas, B. A. (2017, April). Communication-efficient learning of deep networks from decentralized data. In Artificial intelligence and statistics (pp. 1273-1282). PMLR.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes CGPFL, a  cluster generalization framework to enhance better personalization. Existing personalized learning algorithms aim at finding a good enough global model that allows all clients to fine tune. This paper proposes to train K global models to allow for statistical diversity. The paper studies analytically the algorithm, and shows empirical performance.
content.main_review:
The paper addresses an interesting problem of improving FL by localized personalization through clustering. There is an analysis of convergence and a generalization bound. 

The paper has a strong evaluation section against different popular and SoTA algorithms.

Weaknesses: 

- The novelty of the work is misleading. The proposed idea is very similar to HypCluster, introduced by [MMRS20]. HypCluster also clusters users to allow for several global models. Then, in their experimental section, authors combine it with finetuning (this is missing in the related work, that suggest there is no personalization at all in this work). Further, similar regularization techniques are proposed by [SCST18]. 
- Notation changes completely  in section 4.3. making really hard to understand the statements. The notation starts with classic FL notation but then switches to the notation used in [MMRS20].
- It is not clear how to extend this framework to a large number of users. Matrices become too large when N is in the order of millions. The authors could discuss how the algorithm can be adapted to work in practical settings. 
- It is claimed that CGPFL-Heur is intended to avoid tuning the hyperparameter K, but it seems to me that now one has to tune $\mu$. 
- In the experimental side, it would be interesting to see the performance of the algorithm in more naturally federated datasets, like a Stackoverflow, or even EMNIST. 



[SCST18] Smith, V., Chiang, C. K., Sanjabi, M., & Talwalkar, A. (2017). Federated multi-task learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:1705.10467.
[MMRS20] Mansour, Y., Mohri, M., Ro, J., & Suresh, A. T. (2020). Three approaches for personalization with applications to federated learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.10619.
content.summary_of_the_review: In its current states, this paper studies an interesting problem in the field but it still needs to clearly state how this work is novel compared to existing clustering work in FL. Further several sections have to be clarified and notation has to be unified. Experiments are good but could be more representative of realistic FL settings.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer mGxH
content.comment:
1. Q: The novelty of the work is misleading. The proposed idea is very similar to HypCluster, introduced by [MMRS20]. HypCluster also clusters users to allow for several global models. Then, in their experimental section, authors combine it with finetuning (this is missing in the related work, that suggest there is no personalization at all in this work). Further, similar regularization techniques are proposed by [SCST18].

A:  a. Actually, you can find that the personalization method in [MMRS20] is a simple mixture of global model and local model, which is almost same as the approach in [DKMM20] (we refer to as APFL in this paper), while our algorithms using the $L2$-norm to regularize the distance between the generalized model and personalized model. And the purpose of our algorithms are to achieve the optimal personalized federated learning by seeking the optimal generalization-personalization trade-off.

b. The user clustering and data/model interpolation are proposed as three independent personalization methods in [MMRS20]. The user clustering method (HYPCLUSTER) lacks fine-grained personalization while data interpolation (DAPPER) and model interpolation (MAPPER) lack fine-grained generalization. Of course, some direct combinations (HYPCLUSTER+FINETUNE, HYPCLUSTER+DAPPER, and HYPCLUSTER+MAPPER) are discussed in the empirical analysis. However, these simple combinations can hardly provide theoretical guarantee of convergence rate. Moreover, they cannot guarantee to reach the optimal generalization-personalization trade-off because the two processes (e.g., HYPCLUSTER and MAPPER) are not optimized simultaneously.

c. The user clustering (HYPCLUSTER) lacks fine-grained personalization. Using the training loss on the local dataset to measure the grain of personalization, we can get the training loss of the obtained personalized model as $f(\theta_i^\ast)=\min_{\theta_i}\\{ f(\theta_i) + \lambda r(\theta_i, \omega_k^{\ast}) \\}$. If we define the function $g(\theta_i)=f(\theta_i) + \lambda r(\theta_i, \omega_k^{\ast})$, we can obtain that $f(\omega_k^{\ast})=g(\omega_k^{\ast})$. Therefore, we have $f(\omega_k^{\ast})=g(\omega_k^{\ast}) \geq \mathop{\min}_{\theta_i}g(\theta_i)=f(\theta_i^{\ast}) + \lambda r(\theta_i^{\ast}, \omega_k^{\ast})$. That is, $f(\omega_k^{\ast}) \geq f(\theta_i^{\ast}) + \lambda r(\theta_i^{\ast}, \omega_k^{\ast})$, where the function $r(\theta, \omega)=\frac{1}{2}{\lVert \theta-\omega \rVert}^2$ in this paper. This inequality indicates that the personalization of $\theta_i^{\ast}$ is always more fine-grained than the global models $\omega_k^{\ast}$, and the gap becomes larger as the distance between the global model and the personalized model goes larger.

d. Our proposed CGPFL (and CGPFL-Heur) provides theoretical guarantee of convergence rate, which achieves $\sqrt{K}$ times speedup over the state-of-the-art PFL methods. What's more, we demonstrate that the proposed method can reach an optimal generalization-personalization trade-off in PFL, which is the key to optimal personalized federated learning.

e. To assign each client to the cluster, the user clustering method (HYPCLUSTER) requires each client to download all the $K$ global models and computes the losses on these global models, which is expensive for the local devices (especially when the local devices are edge devices). However, we achieve the clustering by conducting k-means++ clustering on the server. 

2. Q: Notation changes completely in section 4.3. making really hard to understand the statements. The notation starts with classic FL notation but then switches to the notation used in [MMRS20].

A: Actually, we explain that the hypothesis $h$ has a direct relationship with the model parameter $\omega$ in Definition 2 in Section 4.3.

3. Q: It is not clear how to extend this framework to a large number of users. Matrices become too large when N is in the order of millions. The authors could discuss how the algorithm can be adapted to work in practical settings.

A: In the proposed framework, the clustering operation is completed on the server, which is usually believed to possess possess computation resources. Of course, when $N$ becomes too large, the computation cost of clustering is a problem. It deserves more explorations on how to reduce the computation cost in the future work.

4. Q: It is claimed that CGPFL-Heur is intended to avoid tuning the hyperparameter $K$, but it seems to me that now one has to tune $\mu$.

A: CGPFL-Heur is designed as a heuristic improvement for CGPFL. It seems that we cannot avoid a hyperparameter ($\mu$) in CGPFL-Heur, but CGPFL-Heur can be much easier than tuning $K$.

[MMRS20] Mansour, Y., Mohri, M., Ro, J., & Suresh, A. T. (2020). Three approaches for personalization with applications to federated learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.10619.
[DKMM20] Deng, Y., Kamani, M. M., & Mahdavi, M. (2020). Adaptive personalized federated learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2003.13461.

content.title: Response to the rebuttal (Part 1/2)
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable comments. Here are our responses to your remaining concerns. Especially, we explain the significance and novelty of this work again. We ask that the reviewer might re-evaluate this paper if this response helps clarify the novelty. Of course, some more questions are welcome if the reviewer has other concerns.

**Q: How this algorithm is meaningful in practice and/or limitations of this work. Number of users, hyperparameters introduced, etc.**

**A:**

**1. Significance:**

1). The proposed algorithm is meaningful for the cases where the local data distributions are of rich diversity, especially when the local data distributions have a cluster structure. In practice, the data on diffenrent devices often tends to be clustered due to geographic location and user preference. For example: for the image classification task, the pictures on the mobile devices of users in the same geographic region usually contains similar objectives while the pictures from distinct regions have dissimilar items; for the next word prediction task, the frequency of each word appears to be similar for users from the same group (e.g., company, lab, family) while the frequency is dissimilar for distinct groups. In these practical cases, the local data tends to be clustered.

2). In federated learning, one of the most important reasons why the clients need to cooperate with other clients is that the data on each client is scarce for training. However, rich data diversity means that some clients are relevant while some are irrelevant. From the perspective of generalization, clustering the relevant clients is needed to achieve fine-grained generalization. From the perspective of personalization, the trained model need to fit the local data distribution as well as possible. Jointly optimizing these two objectives can reach an optimal personalization-generalization trade-off for personalized federated learning. It is exactly what the proposed algorithm does in this work.

**2. Limitation:**

1). **Large $N$**. Although our algorithm conducts clustering on the server, the computation cost of clustering can become high as the number of clients $N$ increases. It is a challenging problem that deserves more efforts in the future.

2). **High-dimension data**. One of the most important limitations of $k$-means clustering is that the computation cost can be expensive when the data is high-dimension (i.e., $d$ is large). In practice, we can select some dimensions to conduct clustering. For example, we can operate on the parameters of fully connected layers while abandoning the parameters of convolutional layers. Of course, in our future work, we will also consider to adopt other efficient clustering methods that can deal with high-dimension data well, such as spectral clustering.

3). **Hyperparameter $K$/$\mu$**. To reach the near-optimal trade-off between personalization and generalization, the hyperparameter $K$/$\mu$ is introduced. In practice, small $K$ is suggested if there isn't any available knowledge. The reason is that small $K$ can already provide more fine-grained generalization than a single global model ($K=1$), meanwhile, small $K$ means that the total data in each group has enough diversity for achieving group generalization.

4). **Generalization bound**. In this work, the generalization bound is mainly introduced as a tool to demonstrate the existence of the optimal personalization-generalization trade-off and to inspire the algorithm to reach a near-optimal trade-off. We only improve the generalization bound, compared with other $L2$-norm regularized PFL methods ([1][2][3][4]). Improving the generalization bound in a more general FL framework can be the future direction.

[1] Li, T., Hu, S., Beirami, A., \& Smith, V. (2021, July). Ditto: Fair and robust federated learning through personalization. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 6357-6368). PMLR.

[2] T Dinh, C., Tran, N., \& Nguyen, T. D. (2020). Personalized Federated Learning with Moreau Envelopes. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 33.

[3] Hanzely, F., \& Richtárik, P. (2020). Federated learning of a mixture of global and local models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.05516.

[4] Hanzely, F., Hanzely, S., Horváth, S., \& Richtarik, P. (2020). Lower Bounds and Optimal Algorithms for Personalized Federated Learning. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 33.

content.title: Response to the rebuttal (Part 2/2)
content.comment:
**Q: Clarifying the paper contributions: clearly separating this work from related work, why previous approaches combined with fine-tuning are different from this, or if this paper formalizes previous approaches already introduced in the literature.**

**A:** The proposed algorithm is distinct from the previous approaches combined with fine-tuning.

| Methods | Single-global | Multiple-global | Optimize two processes |
| :------ | :------ | :------ | :------ |
| Federated learning | e.g., FedAvg [10] | CFL (e.g., [6,12]) | N/A |
| With finetune | FedAvg + Finetune [11] | CFL + Finetune [6] | Successively |
| Global-regularized | e.g., [1,2,3,4] | CGPFL (Ours) | Jointly |

1. **Global model regularized optimization [1,2,3,4] and local fine-tuning are two independent directions for PFL.** As discussed in the exsiting survey papers on FL [7,8,9], global model regularized optimization and local fine-tuning are commonly considered as two independent directions in PFL. Just like the global model regularized optimization [1,2,3,4,5] is distinct from combining FedAvg [10] with local fine-tuning, our algorithm is distinct from combining Clustered FL with local fine-tuning.

2. **Concrete differences.** Our method jointly optimizes the two aspects, i.e., personalization and generalization, by formulating CGPFL as a bi-level optimization problem, while clustering+fine-tuning optimizes the two processes separately. Our proposed CGPFL provides theoretical guarantee of convergence rate, which achieves $\sqrt{K}$ times speedup over the state-of-the-art PFL methods. Moreover, we demonstrate that the proposed method can reach an optimal generalization-personalization trade-off in PFL, which is the key to optimal personalized federated learning. However, the simple combinations (clustering+finetuning) can hardly provide theoretical guarantee of convergence rate and cannot guarantee to reach the optimal generalization-personalization trade-off because the two processes are not optimized simultaneously. For example, the work that you mentioned [6] didn't provide theoretical analysis on convergence rate and generalization-personalization trade-off.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new method by combining clustered FL and personalised FL together. In particular, it simultaneously learns multiple global models by aggregating similar clients within the same cluster, and then conducts personalised modelling for each client.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

1. It is an interesting idea and novel method to do a cluster-enhanced PFL.
2. The proposed method is technique soundness. The detailed convergence rate and generalization error are derived, which is a plus.
This paper is well written.


Weaknesses:

1. Treating each client model as private data is useless.
2. If we simply add a fine-tuning step into the existing clustered FL, they should also work well.
3. The experiments should be enhanced by choosing more personalised FL settings and clustered FL baselines. 


Questions and suggestions:

1. In Algorithm 1, the variables of R and S are not defined. Moreover, in lines 5 and 10, the use of G(.) is inconsistent. The first G uses two matrices as inputs, and the second G uses model parameters w as input. 

2. Why do you choose K-means++ rather than K-means? According to Eq.2, the K-means should be the right one to solve the proposed objective function.

3. The proposed algorithm treats each personalised model as private data, and then updates the generalised model on local clients. However, it seems useless. As stated in Algorithm 1, if the server received the updated generalised model, then it could easily infer the gradient of G(w) which is an L2 distance between the personalised model and the previous generalised model. After that, the server can infer the gradients of the personalised local model /theta. Therefore, the intention of treating personalised models as private data is not achieved. 

4. The global iteration is considered a discrete-time Markov chain. However, the transition matrix Q^t is not a static matrix. How does the Markov chain handle this dynamic transition matrix? Has these dynamics been analysed in any part of the paper?

5. The baseline of FedAvg could be enhanced by incorporating a fine-tuning step to implement personalisation. For example, the paper below has discussed fine-tuning in FL.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.07313

6. As shown in Table 1, the CGPFL has no substantial improvement in comparison with IFCA - a clustered FL method. How about implementing an IFCA with personalised components that simply use IFCA’s final global models to conduct one-step fine-tuning at each corresponding client. Moreover, there are more clustered FL methods that are worth to be compared with.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.10619 

https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.11791 

https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.08647

https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.09749 

 
7. In Fig 3, the optimal K is 12. However, the number of clients is 40. Can you please show the number of clients for each cluster, and then visualise the clusters in a 2D chart? 

8. In Table 2, what if the hyper-parameter lambda varies exponentially?

9. Typos: 
generalizaation (first paragraph in Page 2)
the dimension of P^t should be N*K.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes an interesting method to do cluster-enhanced PFL. However, the experiment is not sufficient to support its claims, and there are some details that need to discussed.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer bgWZ (Part 1)
content.comment:
1. Q: In Algorithm 1, the variables of R and S are not defined. Moreover, in lines 5 and 10, the use of G(.) is inconsistent. The first G uses two matrices as inputs, and the second G uses model parameters w as input.

A: The variable $R$ denotes the number of local iterations to update the generalized model $\omega_k$. To reduce the communication cost, $R$ can be an integer larger than 1. The variable $S$ indicates the number of iterations of the local solver to the upper-level objective: $\min_{\theta_i \in R^d}\\{F_i(\theta_i) := f_i(\theta_i)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\lVert \theta_i-\omega_k^{\ast} \rVert^2\\}$. For the line 5 and 10 in Algorithm 1, you are right. The $\nabla G(\omega_{i,r}^t)$ requires both $\widetilde\theta_i(\omega_{i,r}^t)$ and $\omega_{i,r}^t$ as inputs. Therefore, the line 10 should be written as $\omega_{i,r+1}^t=\omega_{i,r}^t - \beta\nabla_{\omega_i}G(\tilde\theta_i(\omega_{i,r}^t), \omega_{i,r}^t)$. Besides, because the generalizd models are independent from each other and the partial derivatives of $G$ are $\frac{\partial G}{\partial \omega_k}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\in C_k}\frac{\partial r(\theta_i(\omega_k), \omega_k)}{\partial \omega_k}$, which indicates that the gradient $\nabla_{\omega_k}G$ only depends on the corresponding generalized model $\omega_k$. To compute the gradient $\nabla_{\omega_k}G$, we only require $\omega_k$ and $\\{\theta_i|i\in C_k\\}$ as input. In Algorithm 1, $\omega_{i,r}$ is utilized as the local estimation of $\omega_k$. Therefore, $\nabla_{\omega_i}G(\tilde\theta_i(\omega_{i,r}), \omega_{i,r})$ only needs $\tilde\theta_i(\omega_{i,r})$ and $\omega_{i,r}$ as inputs. We have revised the line 10 in the revision paper.

2. Q: Why do you choose K-means++ rather than K-means? According to Eq.2, the K-means should be the right one to solve the proposed objective function.

A: As shown in Algorithm 1, we design our algorithm as an alternating framework. The clustering is conducted at every global round. Taking it into consideration that the fluctuation of the training process, especially during the beginning period (as shown in Figure 4 in appendix C.1), we allow the clustering algorithm to determine the initial centroid points every time we conduct the clustering on the server. In this way, we can dynamically associate the personalized models to the most appropriate generalized model during the training process, to avoid incorrect clustering caused by huge fluctuation in certain round. However, if we choose the initial centroid points in a totally random way (K-means), each personalized model can be associated to the $K$ generalized model with uniform probability. We can believe that the totally random association can make the obtained generalized models deteriorate into the generalized model when $K=1$. Therefore, we adopt K-means++ with certain local client (e.g., client 1) being always associated to the first centroid point, and the other centroid points are chosen by using the motheds in K-means++.

3. Q: The proposed algorithm treats each personalised model as private data, and then updates the generalised model on local clients. However, it seems useless. As stated in Algorithm 1, if the server received the updated generalised model, then it could easily infer the gradient of G(w) which is an L2 distance between the personalised model and the previous generalised model. After that, the server can infer the gradients of the personalised local model /theta. Therefore, the intention of treating personalised models as private data is not achieved.

A: In this work, you can find the privacy is not the focus. We just consider that separating the personalized models and the generalized models, and uploading the generalized models can be helpful for privacy preserving. Of course, the methods in Algorithm 1 is useless in practice. I believe it deserves more explorations in the future work.

4. Q: The global iteration is considered a discrete-time Markov chain. However, the transition matrix $Q^t$ is not a static matrix. How does the Markov chain handle this dynamic transition matrix? Has these dynamics been analysed in any part of the paper?

A: Sorry that we don't analyze this dynamic transition matrix in this paper. We just notice that the global iteration is a discrete-time Markov chain, but we don't solve the optimization problem from the perspective of Markov chain. We believe that this fact may lead to some other approaches to the personalized federated learning framework which can be a future direction.

replying_to: Replying to Reply to Reviewer bgWZ (Part 1)

content.title: Reply to Reviewer bgWZ (Part 2)
content.comment:
5. Q: The baseline of FedAvg could be enhanced by incorporating a fine-tuning step to implement personalisation. For example, the paper below has discussed fine-tuning in FL.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.07313

This work focuses on seeking the optimal personalization-generalization trade-off by solving a bi-level optimization problem, where the personalization and generalization are optimized alternately. By comparison, the fine-tuning step optimizes the personalization after finishing optimizing the generalized models. Therefore, incorporating a fine-tuning step cannot guarantee to reach an optimal personalization-generalization trade-off.

6. Q: As shown in Table 1, the CGPFL has no substantial improvement in comparison with IFCA - a clustered FL method. How about implementing an IFCA with personalised components that simply use IFCA’s final global models to conduct one-step fine-tuning at each corresponding client. Moreover, there are more clustered FL methods that are worth to be compared with.

A: a. Actually, richer statistical diversity the local data distributions are of, larger the advantages of our algorithms can be over the clustered federated learning (e.g., IFCA). For example, we believe the statistical diversity of CIFAR-10 dataset is much richer than MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, so our algorithms obviously outperform IFCA on CIFAR-10 dataset in Table 1.

b. As regard to one-step finetuning, as explained in Q4, simple combinations of IFCA and finetuning can hardly provide theoretical guarantee of convergence rate. Moreover, they cannot guarantee to reach the optimal generalization-personalization trade-off because the two processes (clustering and finetuning) are not optimized simultaneously, while the personalization and generalization are optimized alternately in our method.

7. Q: In Fig 3, the optimal K is 12. However, the number of clients is 40. Can you please show the number of clients for each cluster, and then visualise the clusters in a 2D chart?

A: Sure. We give the clustering results (with K=12, N=40 and DNN model on Fashion-MNIST dataset) in the following table.

     --- Cluster-index ---   User-index   --- 

     -------- 0 ----------- 0, 10, 20, 30

     -------- 1 ----------- 4, 14, 24, 34

     -------- 2 ----------- 7, 17, 27, 37

     -------- 3 ----------- 2, 12, 22, 32

     -------- 4 ----------- 5, 15, 25, 35

     -------- 5 ----------- 3, 13, 23, 33

     -------- 6 ----------- 6, 16, 26

     -------- 7 ----------- 1, 11, 21, 31

     -------- 8 ----------- 28, 38

     -------- 9 ----------- 9, 19, 29, 39

     -------- 10 ---------- 36

     -------- 11 ---------- 8, 18

8. Q: In Table 2, what if the hyper-parameter lambda varies exponentially?

A: As regard to the hyperparameter $\lambda$ in Table 2, we explain in Section 5.4 that the range $\lambda$ is properly chosen to avoid that divergence occurs in pFedMe. We find that when the other hyperparameters are fixed, both too small and too large $\lambda$ can cause the divergence of pFedMe. So the chosen range is almost the largest one.

9. Q: Typos: generalizaation (first paragraph in Page 2) the dimension of $P^t$ should be N*K.

A: We have revised this typo in the revision paper. Many thanks for your suggestions.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2546 by Reviewer 8KAL

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this paper, the authors propose a cluster-based personalized federated learning scheme. More formally, each user is assumed to have a local model $\theta_i$, and these local models are regularized around a number of generalized models $\\{w_k\\}_{k=1}^K$. These generalized models are also determined by solving a $K$-means clustering problem with respect to the local models. In other words, the proposed framework solves a mixture of local and global models, similar to (Hanzely & Richtarik, 2020) or (Li et al., 2021), with the difference that the local models are regularized around solutions of a $k$-means clustering problem which is solved in parallel. 

the authors provide convergence guarantees and generalization bounds as well as numerical experiments to justify their algorithm from both numerical and theoretical point of view.
content.main_review:
I find the idea of the paper interesting and intuitive. However, my main concern is that I cannot fully follow the derivations, mainly due to the inconsistency in the notation. For instance, the function $G$ is introduced to be a function of all models on page 3. But then, I cannot fully follow the notation in Algorithm 1 description, as $G$ seems to have only one generalized model as input. Moreover, in Assumption 2, what is $G_i$ and what is $G_k$? It seems that $G_i$ has something to do with local models, and $G_k$ corresponds to the generalized models, but I am not sure about it. 

Similarly, I am not sure if I understand $\Omega_I$ and $\Omega_K$, defined at the beginning of Section 4. Could you explain them in more detail? It might also be helpful to use different notations (currently, they both use $w_i$).

On a different note, on page 6, the authors claim that Assumption 3 holds as the models are normalized during the training. Note that this could be misleading as normalizing the model will lead to a different algorithm with potentially different convergence properties. In other words, you need to either show the models remain bounded or consider projection/normalization in the analysis. 

Minor comments:
- $P^t \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times K}$ instead of $P^t \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times N}$ in page 4.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I find the idea behind the proposed formulation promising, but I haven't been able to parse the algorithm and the theoretical derivations fully. I have listed my main concerns above, and I am open to raising my score if the authors clarify the theoretical section and algorithm description.

content.title: Reply to reviewer 8KAL
content.comment:
1. Q: The function G is introduced to be a function of all models on page 3. But then, I cannot fully follow the notation in Algorithm 1 description, as G seems to have only one generalized model as input.

A: The function $G$ is exactly a function of all generalized models $\omega_k, k=1,2,...,K$. But these generalizd models are independent from each other and the partial derivatives of $G$ are $\frac{\partial G}{\partial \omega_k}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\in C_k}\frac{\partial r(\theta_i(\omega_k), \omega_k)}{\partial \omega_k}$, which indicates that the gradient $\nabla_{\omega_k}G$ only depends on the corresponding generalized model $\omega_k$. To compute the gradient $\nabla_{\omega_k}G$, we only require $\omega_k$ and $\\{\theta_i|i\in C_k\\}$ as input. In Algorithm 1, $\omega_{i,r}$ is utilized as the local estimation of $\omega_k$. Therefore, $\nabla_{\omega_i}G(\theta_i(\omega_{i,r}), \omega_{i,r})$ only needs $\theta_i(\omega_{i,r})$ and $\omega_{i,r}$ as inputs. Of course, the notation $\nabla G(\omega_{i,r}^t)$ is misleading, we have revised it to be $\nabla_{\omega_i}G(\theta_i(\omega_{i,r}^t), \omega_{i,r}^t)$ in the revision paper.

2. Q: Moreover, in Assumption 2, what is $G_i$ and what is $G_k$? It seems that $G_i$ has something to do with local models, and $G_k$ corresponds to the generalized models, but I am not sure about it.

A: You are right. Because the generalizd models are independent from each other, the function $G$ can be decomposed into $K$ components for the convenience of parallel computation, i.e., $G(\omega_1,...,\omega_K)=\sum_{k=1}^K q_k G_k(\omega_k)$. We know that $G_k(\omega_k)=G_k(\omega_k;\theta_1,...,\theta_j,...)$ is related to several personalized models $\\{\theta_j|j\in C_k\\}$. To compute $G_k(\omega_k)$ in a distributional manner, we utilize $G_i(\omega_k;\theta_j):=p_{k,j}r(\omega_k,\theta_j)$ (where $i\in C_k$) as the local estimation of $G_k(\omega_k)$. So, $G_i(\omega_k)$ depends on the local models.

3. Q: Similarly, I am not sure if I understand $\Omega_I$ and $\Omega_K$, defined at the beginning of Section 4. Could you explain them in more detail? It might also be helpful to use different notations (currently, they both use $\omega_i$).

A: As explained in Question 2, to compute $\omega_k, k=1,2,...,K$ in a distributional manner, we utilize the local updates $\omega_j, j \in C_k$ as the local estimations of $\omega_k$. Therefore, the elements in $\Omega_I$ are the local estimations of the related generalized models in $\Omega_K$. In the revision paper, we use $\\{\omega_{i,R}|i=1,2,...,N\\}$ and $\\{\omega_k|k=1,2,...,K\\}$ to define $\Omega_{I,R}$ and $\Omega_K$, respectively, where $R$ is the number of local iterations.

4. Q: On a different note, on page 6, the authors claim that Assumption 3 holds as the models are normalized during the training. Note that this could be misleading as normalizing the model will lead to a different algorithm with potentially different convergence properties. In other words, you need to either show the models remain bounded or consider projection/normalization in the analysis.

A: In fact, bounding the models are required in the theoretical analysis of convergence rate. The bounded models are necessary for the $\sqrt{K}$ times speedup of the proposed convergence rate. However, the performances of our algorithms in the experimental parts are achieved without any projection/normalization conditions. Therefore, the further theoretical analysis of convergence rate without any projection/normalization conditions (Assumption 3) can be a potential future direction.

5. Minor comments: $P^t \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times K}$ instead of $P^t \in \mathbb{R}^{K\times N}$ in page 4.

A: We have revised this typo in the revision paper. Many thanks for your suggestions.

display_title: Emphasize the novelty and contributions of this paper

content.title: Emphasize the novelty and contributions of this paper
content.comment:
First, we thank for the supportive comments and valuable suggestions from all the reviewers. We would like especially thank the Reviewer 13vq for his/her re-rating of this paper. We have explained for all the concerns on the rebuttal in the latest responses. Of course, some further questions and comments are welcome.

Here, we would like to re-emphasize the novelty and contributions of this paper, which is a significant concern from the Reviewer mGxH.

**Q: Clarifying the paper contributions: clearly separating this work from related work, why previous approaches combined with fine-tuning are different from this paper.**

**A:** The proposed algorithm is distinct from the previous approaches combined with fine-tuning.

| Methods | Single-global | Multiple-global | Optimize two processes |
| :------ | :------ | :------ | :------ |
| Federated learning | e.g., FedAvg [10] | CFL (e.g., [6,12]) | N/A |
| With finetune | FedAvg + Finetune [11] | CFL + Finetune [6] | Successively |
| Global-regularized | e.g., [1,2,3,4] | CGPFL (Ours) | Jointly |

1. **Global model regularized optimization [1,2,3,4] and local fine-tuning are two independent directions for PFL.** As discussed in the exsiting survey papers on FL [7,8,9], global model regularized optimization and local fine-tuning are commonly considered as two independent directions in PFL. Just like the global model regularized optimization [1,2,3,4,5] is distinct from combining FedAvg [10] with local fine-tuning, our algorithm is distinct from combining Clustered FL with local fine-tuning.

2. **Novelty and contributions.** Our method jointly optimizes the two aspects, i.e., personalization and generalization, by formulating CGPFL as a bi-level optimization problem, while clustering+fine-tuning optimizes the two processes separately. Our proposed CGPFL provides theoretical guarantee of convergence rate, which achieves $\sqrt{K}$ times speedup over the state-of-the-art PFL methods. Moreover, we demonstrate that the proposed method can reach an optimal generalization-personalization trade-off in PFL, which is the key to optimal personalized federated learning. However, the simple combinations (clustering+finetuning) can hardly provide theoretical guarantee of convergence rate and cannot guarantee to reach the optimal generalization-personalization trade-off because the two processes are not optimized simultaneously. For example, the work that you mentioned [6] didn't provide theoretical analysis on convergence rate and generalization-personalization trade-off.


[1] Li, T., Hu, S., Beirami, A., \& Smith, V. (2021, July). Ditto: Fair and robust federated learning through personalization. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 6357-6368). PMLR.

[2] T Dinh, C., Tran, N., \& Nguyen, T. D. (2020). Personalized Federated Learning with Moreau Envelopes. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 33.

[3] Hanzely, F., \& Richtárik, P. (2020). Federated learning of a mixture of global and local models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.05516.

[4] Hanzely, F., Hanzely, S., Horváth, S., \& Richtarik, P. (2020). Lower Bounds and Optimal Algorithms for Personalized Federated Learning. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 33.

[5] Yuyang Deng, Mohammad Mahdi Kamani, and Mehrdad Mahdavi. Adaptive personalized federated learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2003.13461, 2020.

[6] Yishay Mansour, Mehryar Mohri, Jae Ro, and Ananda Theertha Suresh. Three approaches for personalization with applications to federated learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.10619, 2020.

[7] Kairouz, P., McMahan, H. B., Avent, B., Bellet, A., Bennis, M., Bhagoji, A. N., ... \& Zhao, S. (2019). Advances and open problems in federated learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:1912.04977.

[8] Tan, A. Z., Yu, H., Cui, L., \& Yang, Q. (2021). Towards personalized federated learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2103.00710.

[9] Kulkarni, V., Kulkarni, M., \& Pant, A. (2020, July). Survey of personalization techniques for federated learning. In 2020 Fourth World Conference on Smart Trends in Systems, Security and Sustainability (WorldS4) (pp. 794-797). IEEE.

[10] McMahan, B., Moore, E., Ramage, D., Hampson, S., \& y Arcas, B. A. (2017, April). Communication-efficient learning of deep networks from decentralized data. In Artificial intelligence and statistics (pp. 1273-1282). PMLR.

[11] Cheng, G., Chadha, K.N., \& Duchi, J.C. (2021). Fine-tuning in Federated Learning: a simple but tough-to-beat baseline. arXiv preprint arXiv:2108.07313v2.

[12] Ghosh, A., Chung, J., Yin, D., \& Ramchandran, K. (2020). An Efficient Framework for Clustered Federated Learning. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 33.

**Thanks again for all the reviewers and the AC for their time and efforts.**
